title: Parallel query processing: bringing data to each operator
lead: Adding machines helps only when matching tuples reach the right place and no single machine does most of the work.
goals: Compare shared-memory, shared-disk, and shared-nothing architectures.
Choose a partitioning strategy that fits the workload.
Estimate broadcast and shuffle costs, and identify bottlenecks.

sections.title: What is shared, and where does parallelism happen?
sections.html:
In a shared-memory architecture, processors share the same RAM address space. In a shared-disk architecture, each node has its own RAM but shares storage. In a shared-nothing architecture, each node has its own CPU, RAM, and disks, and nodes communicate over a network.

Inter-query parallelism runs independent queries concurrently. Within one query, inter-operator parallelism runs different operators at the same time, while intra-operator parallelism divides a scan or join into several pieces. For example, in a pipeline, a scan sends tuples to a filter before the scan has finished. Independent branches of a bushy query plan can also run at the same time.

Source: PDF pages 1–11. The examples and explanations on this learning page were written independently for this learning companion.

Parallelism changes the bottleneck, not the result contract

Latency is elapsed time for one request; throughput is completed requests per unit time at a stated concurrency. Extra workers can improve one without improving the other by the same factor. This course contrasts tightly coupled parallel systems with more geographically/network-separated distributed systems as an architectural convention; the names are not a universal distance-based classification.

Shared memory can contend on memory bandwidth and synchronization. Shared disk needs coordination over common storage and private caches. Shared nothing avoids shared local resources but pays network and distributed-correctness costs for cross-partition work. Startup, skew and coordination prevent assuming linear scaling.

Exercise: three replicas contain the same logical row. Should a transparent SQL scan return it three times?

Worked answer. No. Replicas represent copies of the same logical data, not three extra logical bag rows. Routing or relocating a partition should preserve the logical query result. Data transparency does not guarantee unchanged latency after relocation.

Audit addition: original explanation and worked example. Related evidence: Lecture source · physical PDF pages 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 18, 45.

sections.title: Choosing a partitioning strategy
sections.html:
An application stores orders with customer_id, date, and region fields. If most requests retrieve one customer's orders, hash(customer_id) allows direct routing to the relevant partition. If most requests scan one month's orders, range(date) lets the system skip partitions outside that month. Round-robin partitioning balances the number of rows, but a key lookup usually has to contact several nodes.

If one customer accounts for 40% of the data, partitioning by hash(customer_id) can produce an uneven workload even with a good hash function. Distributing distinct keys evenly does not necessarily distribute tuples evenly. Replication creates additional copies to support availability and reads. Partitioning divides the data into separate pieces to increase capacity and enable parallel processing.

Source: PDF pages 12–19. The examples and explanations on this learning page were written independently for this learning companion.

Balanced row counts can still hide imbalance

Original round-robin example. Assign row numbers 1 through 10 cyclically to three workers, starting at worker 1. Their rows are {1,4,7,10}, {2,5,8}, and {3,6,9}. Counts differ by at most one, but byte sizes, update rates and expensive per-row work can still differ. Hash partitioning keeps equal keys together only with a consistent function and mapping; range partitioning needs non-overlapping, complete boundaries.

Replication of each shard and replication of an entire small table solve different problems. A small Currency table copied to every worker can support local joins with partitioned Orders; its updates still need a consistency policy. Replicas of one Orders shard do not make all other Orders shards locally available. An unrelated-key lookup generally fans out unless a usable secondary index, directory or routing scheme locates the data.

Exercise: ten equal-sized rows are round-robin balanced, but one row takes 100 times more CPU. Is the phase necessarily balanced?

Worked answer. No. Row counts balance storage only under stated assumptions, and do not equalize processing cost or request load. Measure work and bytes as well as tuple counts.

Audit addition: original explanation and worked example. Related evidence: Lecture source · physical PDF pages 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 20, 21.

sections.title: Parallel scans, sorts, and hash joins
sections.html:
Consider 800 GB of data and a read rate of 2 GB/s per machine. One machine needs 800/2 = 400 seconds. With an even split across four machines, each reads 800/4 = 200 GB and takes 200/2 = 100 seconds, excluding startup and network costs. For a range-based sort, machine 1 could hold keys <100 and machine 2 keys ≥100. Sorting locally and then concatenating the results in range order produces a globally sorted result.

A parallel hash join must use the same partitioning function on the join keys of both inputs. A shuffle transfers data between nodes according to the partition key. For example, tuples with join key 42 in R and S must reach the same worker, where a local join can find the matching pairs. Sorting each hash partition locally and concatenating the outputs does not produce a global sort.

Key takeaway

For local joins to find every match, tuples with the same join key must meet at the same worker. Using the same key name is not enough: both inputs need the same partitioning function, partition mapping, and placement of corresponding partitions.

Source: PDF pages 20–26. The examples and explanations on this learning page were written independently for this learning companion.

One join can use three different hash functions

In a parallel hash join, an inter-node partition hash sends matching keys to the same worker. A worker's external partition hash can subdivide inputs for a local Grace join, and its in-memory hash selects a bucket in the build table. Their ranges are determined by different resources: workers, local partitioning buffers, and hash-table memory. They need not use the same number of buckets. At each corresponding join stage, both inputs must use compatible placement for equal keys.

Original parallel sort-merge example. Let R={(20,r1),(75,r2),(130,r3)} and S={(75,s1),(130,s2)}. Partition both at key 100, with keys below 100 at worker 1 and the rest at worker 2. Local sorted joins return (75,r2,s1) and (130,r3,s2). If S instead splits at 50 while R still splits at 100, key 75 is separated: local-only joins lose that pair until data are exchanged.

Exercise: can locally sorted hash partitions be concatenated into a globally sorted answer?

Worked answer. No. Hash bucket order is not key order. For a global ordered result, use ordered non-overlapping ranges and concatenate in their key order, or perform another global merge/order step. Local joins and local sorts do not establish global ordering by themselves.

Audit addition: original explanation and worked example. Related evidence: Lecture source · physical PDF pages 22, 23, 24, 25.

sections.title: Four join scenarios
sections.html:
• If the dimension table is already replicated, join each local fact partition with its local copy of the dimension table.
  • If both inputs are co-partitioned on the same join key with the same mapping, perform local joins.
  • If one input is small, broadcast that input to the workers.
  • If both inputs are large and partitioned on the wrong key, shuffle them by the join key.

Consider R=120 GB, S=1 GB, and 8 workers. Broadcasting means sending a copy of S to the workers. If S already resides on one of the eight workers, this requires approximately 1×7 = 7 GB of network transfer. If tuples are initially distributed uniformly at random, shuffling both R and S is expected to move 7/8 of the total data to a different worker: (120+1)×7/8 = 105.875 GB. This idealized model excludes output and overhead. Broadcasting is suitable only if each worker can store and process S.

Source: PDF pages 27–42. The examples and explanations on this learning page were written independently for this learning companion.

sections.title: The critical path and data skew
sections.html:
Suppose four workers take 3, 3, 3, and 12 seconds. The parallel phase takes at least 12 seconds, rather than the average of (3+3+3+12)/4 = 5.25 seconds. Check for an overloaded partition before adding more machines.

Key takeaway

A parallel phase must wait for its slowest worker. Skew concentrates work in one partition. Adding workers may not help if the heavy partition is still assigned to one worker.

Predicate pushdown and early projection become even more valuable when they also reduce network traffic. State the metric explicitly: total bytes transferred, total CPU work, or wall-clock latency. A plan that reduces total work can still take longer if it concentrates too much work on one worker.

Check your understanding: can two tables hashed on the same key always be joined locally?

No. They also need the same partitioning function and mapping, with corresponding partitions placed together. Having the same key name is not enough.

Source: PDF pages 43–45. The examples and explanations on this learning page were written independently for this learning companion.

quiz.question: Workers take 4, 5, 5, and 15 seconds in one parallel phase. What is the lower bound on the phase duration?
quiz.explanation: The phase must wait for its slowest worker. Coordination and network overhead may increase the total duration further.

source.summary: Lecture 26 compares resource-sharing architectures, levels of parallelism, partitioning and replication, parallel scans, sorts, and joins, and cost models that account for network traffic and skew.
